title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family, ask about someone else's, and use 'my', 'your' and 'of' correctly with masculine, feminine and plural nouns.
intro: Family is at the heart of Sindhi life, and Sindhi has precise words for every relative — your father's brother (چاچو) is not the same as your mother's brother (مامو). In this unit you'll learn the core family words, how to say 'my / your / his', how nouns change for gender and number, and a very Sindhi trick: attaching 'his/her' directly to a noun (**ڀاڻس** bhāṇasi 'his brother').

m. Affectionate/address: بابا bābā, ابا abā.
m. Also a respectful word for an old man.
m · pl پٽ puṭa. Also an affectionate address to any boy or young man: 'puṭa!'
m. His wife: چاچي chāchī. Also any older man, kindly.
f. Also a polite address for an older woman.
m (also used for women). Informal: يار yāru.
m pl. Also خاندان xāndānu 'family, clan'.
f. شادي شده shādī shuda = married.
Agrees with the thing owned: منهنجو (m), منهنجي (f), منهنجا (m pl), منهنجيون (f pl).
Common in writing and careful speech; in conversation also هن جو hun jo.

grammar.title: Gender and plural of nouns
grammar.body:
Every Sindhi noun is **masculine** or **feminine**, and the ending usually tells you which. The plural is made by changing the final vowel:

**Masculine in -o** → plural **-ā**: ڇوڪرو chhokiro → ڇوڪرا chhokirā (boys)
**Masculine in -u** → plural **-a**: پٽ puṭu → پٽ puṭa (sons); ٻار ɓāru → ɓāra (children). The spelling doesn't change — only the final short vowel!
**Masculine in -ū / -ī** → usually no change: ماڻهو māṇhū (person/people), هاري hārī (farmer/farmers).
**Feminine in -ī** → plural **-yūṃ**: ڇوڪري chhokirī → ڇوڪريون chhokiryūṃ
**Feminine in -a / -i** → plural **-ūṃ**: زال zāla → زالون zālūṃ; ڀيڻ → ڀينرون and ڌيءُ → ڌيئرون add -arūṃ.

Most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -ī are feminine, but learn each noun with its gender — it controls the form of 'my', 'of' and adjectives.

grammar.title: 'My', 'your' and 'of': جو / جي / جا / جون
grammar.body:
The word for **'of'** is **جو** (jo), and like منهنجو 'my' it **agrees with the thing possessed**, not with the owner:

جو jo — masculine singular: پيءُ جو گهر 'father's house'
جي jī — feminine singular: پيءُ جي ڪار 'father's car'
جا jā — masculine plural: پيءُ جا ڀائر 'father's brothers'
جون jūṃ — feminine plural: پيءُ جون ڀينرون 'father's sisters'

The owner comes first and takes the **oblique** form, and before a masculine noun with a postposition جو itself becomes جي (je): پيءُ جي گهر ۾ 'in father's house'. The owner's oblique: masculine -u nouns end in -a (دوست جو → dosta jo), -o nouns in -e (ڇوڪري جو chhokire jo 'the boy's'), and pronouns use their oblique (توهان جو, هن جو, اسان جو).

'My' and 'your (intimate)' are single words: **منهنجو / منهنجي / منهنجا / منهنجيون** and **تنهنجو …**. To say 'I have (relatives)', Sindhi simply says 'my brothers are': منهنجا ٻه ڀائر آهن.

examples.en: the boy's name (ڇوڪري here is chhokire, the oblique of ڇوڪرو — same spelling as 'girl'!)

grammar.title: Pronoun endings on nouns: ڀاڻس 'his brother'
grammar.body:
A distinctive feature of Sindhi: possessive pronouns can be **attached to the noun as a suffix** instead of being said separately. This is especially common with family words in everyday speech. The ending **-s / -asi** means 'his / her' and **-m / -ami** means 'my':

ڀاءُ bhāu → **ڀاڻس** bhāṇasi 'his/her brother'
ماءُ māu → **ماڻس** māṇasi 'his/her mother'
پيءُ pīu → **پيڻس** pīṇasi 'his/her father'
ڀيڻ bheṇa → **ڀيڻس** bheṇasi 'his/her sister'
پٽ puṭu → **پٽس** puṭasi 'his/her son'

Note that ماءُ، پيءُ، ڀاءُ insert -ṇ- before the suffix. You don't need to produce these yet — say **سندس ڀاءُ** or **هن جو ڀاءُ** — but you must recognise them, because you will hear them constantly. You'll meet the same idea on verbs in Unit 16.

culture: Sindhi families are often large and close, and several generations may live together or near each other. Relatives are addressed by their kinship title rather than their name — چاچا، مامو، ماسي، ادا، ادي — and these titles are extended to family friends and neighbours as a mark of affection and respect. Cousins are simply called 'brother' and 'sister' (or described as 'my uncle's son'). Elders are never addressed with تون.

lessons.title: My mother, my father

tip.title: "My" agrees with what you own
tip.body:
- **منهنجو** 'my' and **تنهنجو** 'your' (intimate) change with the thing owned, not the owner: منهنجو پيءُ (m) · منهنجي ماءُ (f) · منهنجا ڀائر (m pl).
- **جو** 'of' works the same way: توهان **جو** ڀاءُ, توهان **جي** ڀيڻ, توهان **جا** ڀائر.
- The owner comes first: ڀيڻ جو نالو 'sister's name'.

new: تنهنجي ڀيڻ جو نالو ڇا آهي؟

lessons.title: Sons, daughters and children

tip.title: One child, two children
tip.body:
- Every noun is masculine or feminine, and the plural changes the ending:
- **-o → -ā**: ڇوڪرو → ڇوڪرا · **-ī → -yūṃ**: ڇوڪري → ڇوڪريون
- **-u → -a**, same spelling: پٽ puṭu → puṭa, ٻار ɓāru → ɓāra.
- From two upwards the noun is plural, and 'my' agrees: منهنجا ٻه پٽ.

new: جي ها، هڪ پٽ ۽ ٻه ڌيئرون.
منهنجا ٻه ڀائر ۽ هڪ ڀيڻ آهن.

sentences.en: How many children do you have? (to a friend)

sentences.native: توهان جو پٽ ڪٿي رهي ٿو؟
sentences.roman: tavhāṃ jo puṭu kithe rahe tho?

tip.title: Father's side or mother's side?
tip.body:
- Sindhi has a word for each relative, depending on whose side they're on.
- Father's side: **ڏاڏو / ڏاڏي** grandpa / grandma, **چاچو** uncle, **پڦي** aunt.
- Mother's side: **نانو / ناني** grandpa / grandma, **مامو** uncle, **ماسي** aunt.
- Calling someone, -o becomes -ā: چاچا سائين! 'uncle!'

lessons.title: Married? His wife, her brother

tip.title: His brother: سندس ڀاءُ or ڀاڻس
tip.body:
- 'His / her' = **سندس** before the noun: سندس زال 'his wife', سندس مڙس 'her husband'.
- In speech the ending **-s** is often stuck onto family words: **ڀاڻس** his/her brother, **ماڻس** mother, **پيڻس** father, **ڀيڻس** sister, **پٽس** son.
- You need to recognise these; سندس is always fine to say.
